q: You're about to join a motorway. Which of these road users MUST NOT use it?
options: A van driver
A cyclist
A car towing a caravan
A coach driver
explain: Motorways MUST NOT be used by pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders, riders of motorcycles under 50 cc, certain slow-moving vehicles and agricultural vehicles. Vans, coaches and cars towing caravans may use them.

q: You're a learner driver in England and want some motorway experience before your test. When are you allowed to drive on a motorway?
options: With any supervisor who has held a licence for three years
Only outside rush hours when traffic is light
With an approved driving instructor in a dual-controlled car
Only on motorways that have two lanes
explain: Learner car drivers MUST NOT drive on a motorway unless they're with a DVSA approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls that's displaying L plates (D plates in Wales). It's illegal to practise on the motorway with family or friends.

q: You're driving on a motorway for the first time. Why is it especially important to use your mirrors earlier and look further ahead than on other roads?
options: Motorways have more junctions than other roads
Lane markings are harder to see on motorways
There are more speed cameras on motorways
Traffic is faster, so you have less time to react
explain: Traffic on motorways usually travels faster than on other roads, so you have less time to react. You should use your mirrors earlier and look much further ahead than you would elsewhere.

q: You're on a slip road, about to join a motorway. There's traffic in the left-hand lane. Who has priority?
options: You, as the joining vehicle
Traffic already on the motorway
Whoever is travelling faster
Whichever driver signals first
explain: When you join a motorway you should give priority to traffic already on it. Check the traffic and match your speed so you can fit safely into the flow in the left-hand lane.

q: You're accelerating along a slip road to join a busy motorway. How should you join the traffic in the left-hand lane?
options: Match your speed to fit safely into the flow
Join slowly and expect traffic to move over
Use the hard shoulder until a gap appears
Cross the solid white line as soon as you can
explain: You should check the traffic on the motorway and match your speed to fit safely into the traffic flow in the left-hand lane. Don't cross solid white lines that separate lanes or use the hard shoulder.

q: You're joining a motorway. The slip road doesn't end but carries on as an extra lane on the motorway. What should you do?
options: Move straight into the next lane on your right
Build up speed on the hard shoulder
Cross the solid white line when it's clear
Stay in the lane the slip road becomes
explain: If the slip road continues as an extra lane on the motorway, you should stay in it. Remain in the left-hand lane long enough to adjust to the speed of the traffic before you consider overtaking.

q: You're driving a car on a motorway. There are no signs showing a lower limit. What's the national speed limit for your car?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
80 mph
explain: The national speed limit for cars on a motorway is 70 mph (112 km/h). You MUST NOT exceed it, and signs may show a lower limit.

q: You're towing a caravan on a motorway. No other speed limit is shown. What's the maximum speed you're allowed to drive at?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
40 mph
explain: Cars towing caravans or trailers have a speed limit of 60 mph (96 km/h) on motorways and dual carriageways. The 70 mph motorway limit applies to cars that aren't towing.

q: You're towing a trailer on a three-lane motorway. What does the law say about using the right-hand lane?
options: You may use it only to overtake
You may use it when traffic is light
You MUST NOT drive in it
You may use it if you keep below 50 mph
explain: On a motorway with three or more lanes, you MUST NOT use the right-hand lane if you're drawing a trailer, except in prescribed circumstances.

q: You're following a large lorry on a motorway. Many large vehicles are fitted with speed limiters. What speed might a limiter restrict it to?
options: 46 mph
66 mph
50 mph
56 mph
explain: Many large vehicles are fitted with speed limiting devices that restrict their speed to 56 mph (90 km/h), even on a motorway. You should be patient and only overtake when it's safe.

q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign above the carriageway. What does it mean?
options: Don't use the left lane; 40 mph limit applies
Left lane for slow vehicles; 40 mph advised
Lanes ahead narrow; 40 mph minimum speed
Obstruction ahead; leave at the next exit
explain: The red X means you MUST NOT enter or carry on in the left lane, and a speed shown in a red circle is a mandatory limit. You should move safely to an open lane and keep to the temporary limit.

q: You see this signal at the side of a motorway. What does it show?
options: Minimum speed you must keep to
Number of the next junction
Temporary maximum speed advised
Distance to a hazard in yards
explain: This signal shows a temporary maximum speed advised. A speed limit shown inside a red circle is mandatory, and you MUST NOT exceed it.

q: You're joining a motorway and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: Speed limits here are only advisory
End of the variable speed limit section
Cameras check for drivers using phones
Variable speed limits enforced by cameras
explain: This sign shows that a variable speed limit is in use and is enforced by cameras. Variable speed limit signs change the maximum speed limit on some motorways, and you MUST NOT exceed a limit shown in a red circle.

q: You're driving on a motorway and the signals ahead are showing flashing amber lights. What should you do?
options: Reduce speed and be ready for a hazard
Move into the right-hand lane straight away
Leave the motorway at the next exit
Stop on the hard shoulder and wait
explain: Flashing amber lights warn of a hazard ahead. You should reduce your speed and be prepared for the hazard.

q: You've slowed down on a motorway because the signals were showing flashing amber lights. When can you increase your speed again?
options: As soon as traffic around you speeds up
After one mile if you've seen no hazard
Once you can't see any hazard ahead
After passing a signal that isn't flashing
explain: You should only increase your speed when you pass a signal that isn't flashing, or a sign showing a national speed limit or the word 'END', and you're sure it's safe to do so.

q: You're on a motorway and pass this signal. What does it mean?
options: End of the motorway
Exit lane ends ahead
End of restriction
End of the hard shoulder
explain: This signal means the end of a restriction. You should only increase your speed when you're sure it's safe to do so.

q: You're driving on a motorway and this signal appears above your lane. What MUST you do?
options: Stay in the lane but slow down
Move safely to an open lane
Stop in the lane and wait
Switch on your hazard warning lights
explain: A red X above a lane means you MUST NOT carry on in that lane. You MUST follow the signs to move safely to an open lane. Lane closures shown by red lights are enforced by the police.

q: A lane on the motorway ahead is closed by a red X, but it looks clear. Why is it important not to drive in it?
options: There may be people or stopped vehicles in it
It's being kept free for faster traffic
It's reserved for vehicles leaving the motorway
The road surface has just been painted
explain: A red X identifies a closed lane where people, stopped vehicles or other hazards are present, and there can be several hazards in it. Emergency services and traffic authorities also use closed lanes to reach incidents.

q: You plan to leave the motorway at the next junction, but the left-hand lane is closed by a red X at the exit slip road. What does this mean?
options: You can use the hard shoulder to reach the exit
You can enter the lane just before the exit
You can use the exit if you slow right down
The exit can't be used
explain: Where the left lane is closed at an exit slip road, the exit can't be used. You MUST NOT drive in a closed lane, so carry on to the next exit.

q: On a motorway, the signals ahead show red flashing lights and every lane is shown as closed. What MUST you do?
options: Use the hard shoulder to pass the closure
Drive slowly past in the left-hand lane
Stop and not go beyond the signal
Reverse back to the last exit
explain: When red flashing lights show all lanes closed, the road is closed. You MUST NOT go beyond the sign in any lane or use the hard shoulder to avoid the closure unless a police or traffic officer directs you to. You MUST NOT reverse on a motorway.

q: You see this signal above your lane on a motorway. What does it mean?
options: Change lane
Leave the motorway here
Hard shoulder now open
Slow vehicles keep left
explain: This signal tells you to change lane in the direction the arrow shows. Use your mirrors and move over when it's safe.

q: You're driving on a motorway and see this signal. What does it mean?
options: Two-way traffic ahead
Hard shoulder open as a lane
Slip road joins from the right
Lane ahead closed
explain: This signal warns that a lane ahead is closed. You MUST follow the signs in advance of a closed lane to move safely to an open lane.

q: A motorway signal shows the word 'Fog', but the road ahead looks clear. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the fog has probably cleared
Be prepared for a bank of fog ahead
Switch on your rear fog lights now
Speed up to get past before the fog
explain: If 'Fog' is shown on a sign but the road is clear, be prepared for a bank of fog or drifting patchy fog ahead. You MUST NOT use fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced.

q: You're driving on a clear three-lane motorway with no slower traffic ahead. Which lane should you use?
options: The middle lane
The right-hand lane
Any lane, if you keep to the limit
The left-hand lane
explain: You should keep in the left lane unless you're overtaking. If you've overtaken, return to the left lane when it's safe to do so.

q: You're overtaking a lorry on a motorway and plan to move back into the left lane. What should you make sure of?
options: That you've reached at least 70 mph
That you don't cut in on the lorry
That the lorry driver flashes you in
That you keep signalling right
explain: When you've overtaken, return to the left lane when it's safe, making sure you don't cut in on the vehicle you've just overtaken.

q: You're in the left-hand lane of a motorway. Ahead, a recovery vehicle is helping a broken-down car on the hard shoulder. What should you do if it's safe?
options: Sound your horn to warn them you're passing
Slow right down to see what's happening
Move into the next lane to give them space
Flash your headlights at the recovery driver
explain: Be aware of recovery workers and stopped vehicles on the hard shoulder or in an emergency area. If you're in the left lane and it's safe, move into the adjacent lane to create more space between you and them.

q: You're in the middle lane of a motorway, behind a slower car that's also in the middle lane. The left-hand lane is clear. What should you do?
options: Move into the left lane to pass it
Overtake on the right when it's safe
Flash your headlights so it moves over
Stay close behind until it moves left
explain: You should overtake only on the right. Don't overtake on the left or move to a lane on your left to overtake.

q: You're in slow, congested motorway traffic. The lanes are moving at similar speeds, but your lane on the left is moving slightly faster than the lane to your right. What should you do?
options: Keep up with the traffic in your lane
Change to the lane on your right
Weave between lanes to make progress
Use the hard shoulder to get ahead
explain: In congested conditions, traffic in left-hand lanes may sometimes move faster than traffic to the right. You may keep up with the traffic in your lane, even if this means passing traffic on your right, but don't change lanes unnecessarily or weave in and out.

q: You're approaching a motorway junction. Signs show that the left-hand lane leads directly off the motorway. When should you get into that lane?
options: Whenever it has less traffic than the others
When you need to overtake slower vehicles
As soon as you see the first sign
Only if you want to go the way it leads
explain: At some junctions a lane may lead directly off the motorway. Only get into that lane if you wish to go in the direction shown by the signs or road markings.

q: Traffic on the motorway is moving very slowly and the hard shoulder beside you is empty. It isn't being used as an extra lane. When may you drive on it?
options: When the left lane is at a standstill
To reach your exit more quickly
Only in an emergency or if directed to
When there are no vehicles on it
explain: You MUST NOT use a hard shoulder except in an emergency, or if you're directed to by the police, traffic officers or a traffic sign.

q: You're on a motorway where the hard shoulder can be used as an extra lane at busy times. When can you drive in it?
options: When a red X is displayed above it
When a speed limit is shown above it
When the sign above it is left blank
Whenever the traffic becomes heavy
explain: You can only use the hard shoulder as an extra lane when a speed limit is shown above it. A red X or a blank sign above the hard shoulder means you MUST NOT use it except in an emergency.

q: You're driving on a motorway with no hard shoulder. How will you recognise an emergency area?
options: Green signs showing a white letter P
Blue signs with an orange SOS telephone
Yellow signs showing a breakdown truck
Red signs with a white warning triangle
explain: Emergency areas are marked by blue signs with an orange SOS telephone symbol and may have orange surfacing. They MUST only be used in an emergency.

q: You're driving on a motorway and begin to feel sleepy. What should you do?
options: Stop on the hard shoulder for a short nap
Pull into an emergency area and rest
Stop at a service area or leave at an exit
Open a window and carry on to your destination
explain: If you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place, but not in an emergency area or on the hard shoulder. Service areas are provided for breaks, and rest facilities may also be reached from motorway exits.

q: You stopped in an emergency area after your car developed a fault. It's now been fixed. How should you rejoin the motorway?
options: Build up speed and pull out into a gap
Phone the operator and follow their advice
Use hazard lights and pull out slowly
Wait until the lane beside you is empty
explain: To rejoin the carriageway from an emergency area, you MUST use the emergency telephone provided and follow the operator's advice. A lane may need to be closed so that you can rejoin safely.

q: You're ready to rejoin the motorway from the hard shoulder after a breakdown. What should you do?
options: Build up speed, signal and watch for a safe gap
Pull straight into the left lane at low speed
Switch on your hazard lights and pull out
Wait for a driver to flash you out
explain: To rejoin from a hard shoulder, build up speed, indicate and watch for a safe gap in the traffic. Be aware that vehicles, obstructions or debris may be on the hard shoulder.

q: You realise you've just missed your exit on the motorway. What should you do?
options: Reverse along the hard shoulder
Stop on the hard shoulder to check a map
Carry on to the next exit
Cross the central reservation
explain: If you've missed your exit or taken the wrong route, carry on to the next exit. You MUST NOT reverse, cross the central reservation or drive against the traffic flow.

q: You're driving on a motorway when your mobile phone rings. It's an important call you've been expecting. What should you do?
options: Stop on the hard shoulder to answer it
Pull into an emergency area to answer it
Answer it quickly while holding the phone
Call back when parked at a service area
explain: Don't stop on any part of a motorway, including the hard shoulder or an emergency area, to make or receive phone calls, except in an emergency. You MUST NOT use a hand-held phone while driving.

q: You're driving along a motorway slip road and see someone hitchhiking at the side of the road. What does the law say?
options: You MUST NOT stop to pick them up
You may pick them up if you use hazard lights
You may stop on the hard shoulder for them
You may stop briefly at the end of the slip road
explain: You MUST NOT pick up or set down anyone on a motorway, except in an emergency. Pedestrians MUST NOT be on motorways or slip roads except in an emergency.

q: You're in the middle lane of a motorway and want to leave at the next junction. What should you do?
options: Stay in the middle lane until the last marker
Move into the left-hand lane well before your exit
Cut across to the slip road at the last moment
Slow down in the middle lane before the exit
explain: Watch for the signs telling you you're getting near your exit and move into the left-hand lane well before you reach it. Signal left in good time and reduce your speed on the slip road as necessary.

q: You're approaching an exit on a motorway and see these countdown markers. About how far from the exit is the marker with three bars?
options: 300 yards
150 yards
3 miles
600 yards
explain: Countdown markers show the distance to an exit from the motorway. Each bar represents about 100 yards, so the three-bar marker is about 300 yards from the exit.

q: You've just left a motorway after driving at 70 mph for a long time. Why should you check your speedometer?
options: Your speedometer may read high after a long run
Slip roads have a higher limit than motorways
Your tyres will be hotter than usual
You may be going faster than you realise
explain: On leaving a motorway your speed may be higher than you realise; 50 mph may feel like 30 mph. Check your speedometer and adjust your speed, as some slip roads and link roads have sharp bends.

q: You're driving on a motorway at night. What colour are the reflective studs between the carriageway and the central reservation?
options: Amber
Red
Green
White
explain: Amber studs mark the central reservation of a dual carriageway or motorway. Red studs mark the left edge of the road and white studs mark the lanes.

q: You're driving at night on a motorway. Which colour reflective studs mark the left-hand edge of the carriageway?
options: White
Green
Amber
Red
explain: Red studs mark the left edge of the road. Amber studs mark the central reservation, and green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at slip roads and lay-bys.

q: You're driving on a motorway at night and see green reflective studs on your left. What do they mark?
options: The edge of the central reservation
The lines between the motorway lanes
Where a slip road joins or leaves
Temporary lane layouts at road works
explain: Green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.

q: You're driving through road works on a motorway at night and see green/yellow reflective studs. What do they show?
options: The edge of a slip road or lay-by
Temporary changes to the lane layout
The edge of the central reservation
A lane for works vehicles only
explain: Green/yellow studs indicate temporary adjustments to lane layouts, for example where road works are taking place. Lanes at road works may be narrower than normal, so keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front.

q: Your car develops a problem on a motorway and you can't reach an exit or a service area. Where should you try to stop?
options: In an emergency area or on the hard shoulder
In the right-hand lane by the central reservation
In the lane you're in, with hazard lights on
On the verge of the central reservation
explain: If you can't leave at the next exit or reach a service area, move into the left lane and pull into an emergency area or onto a hard shoulder if you can. Stop as far to the left as possible, with your wheels turned to the left.

q: You're pulling onto the hard shoulder because your car has developed a fault. If you can, where should you stop?
options: Just before an exit slip road
Under a bridge for shelter
Just beyond an emergency telephone
Halfway between two emergency telephones
explain: If you can, stop just beyond an emergency telephone, as far to the left as possible and leaving space to get out. Switch on your hazard warning lights.

q: You've stopped on the hard shoulder after a breakdown. How should you and your passengers get out of the car?
options: Through the driver's door, facing the traffic
Through whichever door is nearest to you
Through the rear door on the traffic side
Through the doors on the side away from traffic
explain: Leave your vehicle by the side furthest from traffic, if it's safe and possible to do so, and make sure your passengers do the same. Then get well away from the vehicle and moving traffic.

q: Your car has broken down on the hard shoulder and you're waiting for help behind the safety barrier. It starts to rain heavily. What should you do?
options: Get back into your car to keep dry
Stay where you are, away from the car
Shelter behind the open boot of the car
Stand in front of the car, out of the wind
explain: Wait well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, behind the safety barrier where there is one. DO NOT return to your vehicle, even if it's raining, cold or dark.

q: Your car breaks down in a live lane of a motorway. You can't get it to the left lane and it isn't safe to get out. What should you do?
options: Stay in the car, keep your belt on and call 999
Get out and push the car onto the hard shoulder
Put a warning triangle behind the car
Stand behind the car to wave traffic past
explain: If you can't get your vehicle to the left lane or a place of relative safety and can't get out safely, stay in it with your seat belt and hazard warning lights on. Call 999 immediately and ask for the police, or press your SOS button if your vehicle has one.

q: You've broken down on a motorway and are calling for help on your mobile phone. How can you give your exact location?
options: Describe the nearest bridge or building
Quote the details on a nearby marker post
Tell them how many lanes the motorway has
Read out your car's registration number
explain: Quote the numbers and letters on the marker posts or driver location signs along the edge of the road. You can also use a mobile phone mapping app, or press your vehicle's SOS button if it has one.

q: You've stopped on the hard shoulder with a puncture in a tyre on the traffic side of your car. What should you do?
options: Change the wheel yourself as quickly as you can
Change it if you wear high-visibility clothing
Change it with your hazard lights switched on
Leave it and call for help from a safe place
explain: You should not attempt repairs on your vehicle on a motorway. Get well away from it and moving traffic, then use the emergency telephone or contact a breakdown recovery service.

q: You're driving on a motorway when a box falls off your roof rack onto the carriageway. What should you do?
options: Stop somewhere relatively safe and call 999
Stop on the hard shoulder and walk back for it
Reverse along the hard shoulder to collect it
Drive on, as someone else will move it
explain: If anything falls from your vehicle onto a motorway, DO NOT try to remove it yourself. Stop in a place of relative safety and call the emergency services on 999.

q: You're driving on a motorway when the traffic ahead slows suddenly because of a queue. Why might you briefly switch on your hazard warning lights?
options: To show you're about to change lanes
To warn drivers behind you of the hazard
To thank a driver who let you in
To tell the driver ahead to move over
explain: You MUST NOT use hazard warning lights while driving unless you're on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway and need to warn drivers behind you of a hazard or obstruction ahead. Only use them long enough for your warning to be seen.

q: You're approaching road works on a motorway where a lane is closed. Traffic is queuing and moving very slowly. What should you do?
options: Merge in turn when it's safe
Change lanes to pass the queue
Drive along the coned-off area
Use the hard shoulder to get past
explain: Where lanes are restricted due to road works, merge in turn when it's safe. Merging in turn is recommended when traffic is moving at very low speed, but not at high speed. Don't switch lanes to overtake queuing traffic or drive through an area marked off by cones.

q: On a motorway you come up behind a slow-moving works vehicle showing this sign on its back. What MUST you do?
options: Stop behind it until it moves off
Pass on whichever side is clearer
Pass it on the side the arrow shows
Follow it until the next junction
explain: Where a 'Keep Left' or 'Keep Right' sign is shown on the back of a works vehicle, you MUST move over and pass it on the side indicated. Don't return to the closed lane until you can see it's safe.

q: At motorway road works, you're behind a vehicle displaying the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING'. What MUST you do?
options: Overtake on the right when it's clear
Flash your lights so it pulls over
Stay behind and don't pass it
Pass it using the hard shoulder
explain: Where a vehicle displays the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING', you MUST NOT pass it.

q: You're about to enter a contraflow system at motorway road works. What should you do?
options: Speed up to clear it quickly
Slow down and leave a bigger gap
Close up on the vehicle in front
Move nearer the oncoming traffic
explain: In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal, with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic. At the start and finish, slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front, as changes in the camber of the road may affect your vehicle's stability.

q: Your car breaks down while you're driving through road works on a motorway. If one is available, where should you move it?
options: Into a signed road works refuge
Into the area coned off for the works
Onto the central reservation
Into the nearest closed lane
explain: If you break down in road works, follow the usual breakdown advice, but remember that areas marked off by cones contain significant hazards. Where available, move your vehicle into a signed road works refuge location.

q: You're driving along a main road and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Motorway services on the M62 ahead
End of motorway regulations on the M62
Start of motorway; motorway rules apply
Diversion route for traffic on the M62
explain: This sign shows the start of a motorway and the point from which motorway regulations apply. For example, from here you MUST NOT stop except in an emergency.
